paragraphs: Another autumn came, and the reeds on both banks of the Fei River turned white early. At the first gust, their light down drifted over the opposing stockades and into the soldiers' bowls. The dead at Baishi had scarcely been buried, and the two government signboards still hung outside the county office, when Liu Yu gathered his light craft downstream. In daylight the boats looked no different from fishing skiffs carrying firewood. By night their masts were lowered; with a few men crouched behind the gunwales, they passed without startling even the waterbirds in the reeds.

He Wuji spread the river patrol reports before a candle. Qin’s newly built western granary stood east of the old relay station, the main road to its north and low paddy fields to its south. A ditch protected the main gate, but behind the compound ran a shallow channel apparently impassable to boats. Qin cavalry patrolled often, yet sentries still changed watches according to the schedule of the roads. When the water rose, the silt was deep; no one had sounded that channel properly.
“The granary commander is careful,” He Wuji said. “Last night he carried his own lantern twice around the camp.”
Liu Yu studied the crooked line of water on the map. “Careful on land alone is not careful enough.”
“And if we cannot burn all the grain?”

“Burn the timber for his storehouses and destroy his firefighting gear. Let him learn that grain sacks are not safe simply because they stand behind walls. Once we’ve struck, leave. Don’t waste men at the gate.”

A commandant asked to take another hundred men; Liu Yu refused. The skiffs could not carry so many, and even if they could, they would lose their speed. A soldier newly returned from fighting Sun En at sea volunteered to find the route, claiming he knew water. On questioning, he knew tides but had never entered the Fei’s shallow channels. Liu Yu ordered him to remain on the southern bank with the support party. The man protested. He Wuji pointed to the sandbars on their mud map and asked him to identify them. After naming two incorrectly, the soldier withdrew on his own to load the boats.

Fog came in the latter half of the night. Liu Yu led the first boat, its oars wrapped in worn hemp, their tips entering the black water almost soundlessly. As they passed a patch of flattened reeds, a hand suddenly rose from the mud and seized the gunwale. A soldier raised his blade in fright, but it was a scout sunk into the riverbed, only his shoulders above the surface. Two men hauled him aboard; the skiff listed and water surged into its hull. Liu Yu gripped the side until the others had steadied it, then let go.

A Qin patrol lantern was already moving along the embankment. An old sentry on the bank sneezed and spat into the water. All the men lay still, not daring even to wipe away the cold water that had splashed inside their collars. Once the light had passed, two short heron calls came back from the lead boat. The skiffs reached shore one by one. The first men out sank ankle-deep in mud and scrambled up the bank with their weapons held high.

A crossbow bolt struck the first guard as he turned to sound the gong. The second ran for the granary gate with a long saber, but He Wuji slammed into him from the side and they rolled together down the earthen slope. The blade ripped He Wuji’s sleeve before another soldier pinned the man’s shoulder. Beyond them lay the grain stacks. Qin troops were already on their feet, and a granary clerk, wearing only half his armor, shouted through the firelight, “Backs to the granary wall! Nobody run to save his own baggage!”

These were not men who scattered at the first assault. Qin soldiers formed two ranks, spears protruding over shield rims. Three Beifu men fell beneath the gallery in their first rush at the gate. Liu Yu did not send more to force it. Instead he led a party around the rear wall, tossed a hooked rope into a dead locust tree, and climbed over into the yard where empty barrels and cart axles were stored. Wooden wheels stood in rows; oiled shafts lay beneath a shed. He ordered the oil jars emptied and the fire lit there.

The timber caught first; only afterward did flames lick the granary wall. The unit leader defending the storehouse smelled burning and turned to see the rear yard glowing red. He detached men to move the grain and took the rest to block the back gate. Even in the confusion, voices called out damage by storehouse number. Liu Yu heard in them the same maddening calm with which Beifu men counted boats and reported arrows.
“Leave the east gate open,” he ordered. “Once we’ve burned enough, we’re gone.”
One Beifu soldier started after a fleeing defender carrying a sack of grain. Liu Yu seized him by the neck guard. “Did you come to seize grain or collect heads?”

Around dawn, thick smoke rose from the western granary. Qin horsemen arrived to find only a few lengths of rope in the crossing channel. Half the grain was saved from the flames; the other half was waterlogged and would mold unless dried at once. The death register listed fourteen defenders and seven Jin soldiers. An empty skiff lay abandoned in the rear yard. The Qin men counting their losses did not mistake its capture for victory. Carved into its bottom was the mark of a Jingkou carpenter. A boatman among them recognized it but dared say nothing.

Three days later, a bridge downstream collapsed. Heavy rain had fallen the night before, and Qin guards at the bridgehead assumed the flood had worn through its cables. As they stripped off their armor to enter the water, three men armed with knives emerged from beneath the piers and cut the remaining ropes. The floating timbers broke apart. Qin crossbowmen fired after the escaping skiffs, wounding two boatmen, but could not save the bridge. On the fifth day, a grain convoy rounded a narrow bend. Men stood on the field ridges holding hoes, apparently draining the paddies. When they opened a gap in the bank, the sudden current swept the lead vessel sideways; Beifu troops rushed out of the reeds, seized seven boats, and burned four.

Liu Yu paid for these successes. When wounded men were carried back to Jingkou, some had legs so badly infected that they could no longer stand. Fire oil was running short and boat timber was harder to obtain. He Wuji opened the casualty and supply accounts and urged a pause in the raids. Liu Yu told him to inspect the captured grain first. Half was still damp and had to be spread out to dry in a courtyard. Armored men laughed around their newly captured rice sacks, while Liu Yu worried over how many sacks would ever provide an edible meal.

On the seventh day the Beifu Army entered a small riverside town. Six hundred Qin troops had garrisoned it under a Di commander surnamed Xin, whose left shoulder bore an old arrow wound. The men who opened the gate were formerly registered as Jin soldiers and had families on the southern bank. They first burned the northern corner tower, forcing the defenders to divide, and only then unbarred the gate. Entering town, Liu Yu ordered the axemen to remain outside. Most civilians kept their doors shut even as people gathered in the streets. He did not treat those who had opened the gate as speaking for the entire town.

General Xin was brought out, blood staining his armor, still cursing the gate-openers for breaking their oath to defend the town. Liu Yu had his bonds cut and permitted him to take his surviving troops and wounded north. Xin looked at several doors that had never opened and said there were people here who wished to remain citizens of Qin. Liu Yu heard him. Better, he answered, to wait until people chose to open their doors than to lock everyone inside.

Before leaving, the defeated commander knelt at the threshold and picked up the broken wooden tablet of his unit, trampled underfoot. “General Liu, you are letting me go. Once I return to the northern camp, we shall fight again.”
“I know.”
“Then why release me?”

Liu Yu glanced at the wounded in the town and ordered the army physicians to take two of Xin’s gravely injured men along with them. “Killing you today will not add one measure of grain to the stores.”

A Jin banner replaced the Qin flag on the wall. Some townspeople cheered at the wharf; others quietly pushed their Qin land-allotment vouchers into their stoves, then, unable to bear it, hooked them out with sticks before they had finished burning. The grain-levy official asked whether, now that the town had been restored, he might immediately collect three months of military provisions under Jin regulations. Liu Yu ordered him first to record what grain actually existed. Changing a flag, he said, could not conjure food out of an empty storehouse.

Over the next dozen days Beifu boats appeared and vanished among the channels. The army seized two small towns, burned several grain sheds, and broke two pontoon bridges. Some riverside forts opened at the sight of Jin banners; others took down their Qin signs but locked their gates against everyone. A handful of southern-born soldiers deserted Qin camps. Their numbers were small, but the talk they provoked was not. Some officers requested village searches and the detention of every able-bodied man; others demanded five thousand cavalry to capture Liu Yu within three days. Memorials crowded the imperial desk. Fu Jian merely spread out the river map and placed each battle report on the site where the loss had occurred.

Fu Rong pointed at two burned granaries. “They’re far apart, but boats can reach both. Liu Yu hasn’t attacked our principal camp. He wants us to rush to every fire, until he has dragged our cavalry into the flooded fields.”
“Why was the granary ditch empty?” Fu Jian suddenly asked.

The quartermaster claimed that rain had filled it with silt. Fu Rong threw a mud-stained work-levy tally at his feet. The laborers assigned by the court to excavate the ditch had worked only three days before being diverted to build a wall around a relative’s estate. Most of the felt mats issued against fire were old and fell apart when wet. Two sections of the reserve wooden bridge entered in the register had never been built.
“Liu Yu has skill,” Fu Rong said. “But if the ditch had been dug and the sentries posted properly, he’d have lost several more men before he got inside tonight.”

The official’s seal was taken from him. Fu Jian forbade an immediate execution. Granary supplies, labor assignments, and fodder accounts were to be sealed and sent to the Secretariat and army command for joint examination. Someone asked how the troops could be kept vigilant unless the man was killed at once. Fu Jian opened the military code and ordered him to distinguish the evidence required for stealing army grain from that required for collusion with an enemy in battle. If his own anger were enough to convict, he said, someone else could convict him the same way tomorrow.

Fu Rong then reorganized the defenses. Only three main bridge routes were to remain; the rest would be dismantled. Central-army units would rotate through the granaries, replacing scattered locally levied soldiers. Boats would be numbered, and anyone who privately seized civilian craft would be disciplined. Cavalry were withdrawn from the low embankments, leaving the channels to infantry and boatmen. Three upstream ferries were reinforced with timber forts; passing merchant vessels were to have their numbers and cargoes registered. Civilian salt, medicine, and ordinary rice were still to pass according to regulation. Inspections required time, so boatmen were to be given crossing windows, and no one was to extort payment under cover of a search.

An angry young prince said they were afraid of Liu Yu, yielding ground first despite having more soldiers. Fu Jian refused to boast. “When five thousand horsemen sink into a paddy, what will their horses eat? Follow those blue lines on the map all the way through before you ask to fight.” The young man had ridden half a li of muddy road only the previous day and knew how deep the ruts were. Nevertheless he felt humiliated, and gripped his sword hilt for a long time as he received the order.

Others urged that all southern-born Qin soldiers be disarmed and transferred. Fu Jian ordered army clerks to count how many had sent letters south and how many had married and established households within Qin territory. Those who wished to lay down their arms and return home were to receive their lawful pay and rations; their military-household land vouchers must not be confiscated. Someone feared that even more men would flee. Fu Jian answered that if a soldier held a sword while thinking only of home, and they waited until battle to release him, his comrades would be the ones to take arrows in his place.

When copies of these orders reached Liu Yu, the Beifu men had just divided their captured grain. Liu Yi heard that Qin had pulled back its forward posts and laughed that the northerners were frightened; he proposed burning the new crossing at night. But He Wuji produced leave requests from the ferry boatmen. Several men who routinely carried Beifu grain now refused to sail upstream. They said Qin neither confiscated cargoes nor prohibited transport, but by recording every vessel’s point of origin and hour of passage, it seemed to be entering future trouble into a ledger.
“Offer them twice the price,” Liu Yi said.

“Money isn’t what frightens them,” He Wuji replied. “The Qin forts will still be there tomorrow. We may be here today and gone the next. If they’re made to confess whom they carried rice for, their families still live on the other bank.”

Liu Yu ordered the clerks to assemble ten days of figures for each unit: grain consumed, sick and wounded, boats lost. Burning one Qin granary might cost ten jars of oil, two or three boats, and several old soldiers who knew the waterways. Holding one captured town meant leaving men to guard it and feeding households whose hearths had gone cold. His officers reported victories every day. The grain ledger grew thinner every day.

Early the next morning, a Beifu soldier dropped a sack while carrying grain, scattering millet across the wet earth. He knelt to gather it. Others laughed that he could care about a few kernels. Liu Yu went over and crouched beside him, lifting a handful. When he shook his palm, sand and mud sifted between his fingers; even what remained might not be fit to eat.
“Take a town and someone must defend it. Defend its people and you must have rice,” he told He Wuji. “The Qin have fallen back not to leave us a road, but to make us pave it with grain.”

Another mounted scout galloped into town with news that Qin had raised a new camp west of Shiliang Ferry, garrisoned by fewer than two thousand men. The river there was wide, but a strip of higher, dry ground ran beside it. To attack, Beifu troops would have to drag their skiffs into an exposed landing place beneath Qin crossbows already deployed above. Liu Yi urged a night assault; He Wuji hesitated. Liu Yu drew two withdrawal lines across the dry ground on the map. He ordered surplus troops pulled out of the two newly captured towns, the wounded returned to the southern bank, the skiffs concentrated once more, and all fire oil issued through central command alone.
“Those towns were hard won,” Liu Yi protested, stopping him outside the county office. “How many days have our banners even flown there?”
“What use are banners above the walls if the people beneath them starve?” Liu Yu replied. “If they’re waiting for us at Shiliang Ferry, we cannot arrive at the hour they’ve chosen.”

As the troops withdrew, some townspeople ran after them, asking whether the Qin would settle accounts when they returned. Liu Yu promised to notify the Qin authorities by envoy of those who had opened the gates; any unauthorized reprisals would be entered in the joint verification registers kept by both armies. A junior county clerk doubted that two states would really record the fate of one gate-opener. Liu Yu told him to write down his name and address, gave a copy to He Wuji, and ordered it enclosed in the next letter exchanged across the river.

After dusk, the Beifu skiffs gathered in a concealed inlet on the southern bank. A scout who had previously sounded the route came with a length of wet rope and reported that the shallows had dropped another three inches overnight. Liu Yu told him to measure the depth. An old soldier laughed that they must be planning another secret crossing. Liu Yu counted the knots again and replied that with most grain boats now inspected, stealing up to a few more granaries by night would no longer be enough.

The river wind chilled the wet rope. To the west, the lights of Qin camps appeared one by one. Through the reeds, men returning to camp carried a damaged skiff past a village. An old woman asked the Jin soldiers which country’s frontier they were defending, exactly. One man stared, then answered that they defended the south. She pointed to wheat still standing in the field: if the south meant to defend itself all the way here, who would harvest her wheat tomorrow? The soldier said nothing. He only bent down, picked up her sickle from where it had fallen beside a field ridge, and set it back by her door.

Three days later, Qin rotated its upstream guards and raised two more command platforms behind the lines. The Beifu boats ceased their night attacks. But both banks knew what had happened: Liu Yu had assembled his skiffs, and Fu Jian had drawn up his army on dry land. Mist rose from the river, dampening the edges of their banners. The watch sounded three times. No one mistook it for peace.
